system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2182-06-27 00:53:00 to 2182-07-03 15:44:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with stage IV cholangiocarcinoma on chemotherapy, was readmitted with fever and found to have recurrent E. coli bacteremia. Initial evaluation revealed no abdominal pain, but elevated liver enzymes prompted an ERCP, which identified a blocked bile duct. A plastic stent was removed and metal stents cleaned. Due to persistent obstruction, a percutaneous transhepatic biliary drain (PTC drain) was placed, with pus noted, confirming cholangitis. Microbiology revealed the E. coli strain was resistant to ertapenem, necessitating a switch to IV meropenem for a 10-day course. He remained afebrile, with improving labs, and was discharged home with IV antibiotics via PICC line, oral vancomycin for C. diff prophylaxis, and instructions for drain care. Follow-up was arranged with oncology and interventional radiology.
problems: Malignant neoplasm of extrahepatic bile ducts
Other and unspecified Escherichia coli [E. coli]
Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus
Hypertrophy (benign) of prostate without urinary obstruction and other lower urinary tract symptom (LUTS)

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ year old man with metastatic cholangiocarcinoma, s/p biliary
stents and external biliary drain, with persistent fever and improving LFTs 
// please eval for hepatic abscess

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were obtained from the lung bases to the pubic
symphysis after administration of 130 cc of IV Omnipaque contrast.  Oral
contrast was not administered.  Axial images were interpreted in conjunction
with coronal and sagittal reformats.

DLP:  585 mGy-cm

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS: 

The visualized heart is normal.  No pericardial effusion. Bilateral lower lobe
opacities are most consistent with atelectasis. No pleural effusion.

ABDOMEN:

The gallbladder is distended with new wall edema and pericholecystic
stranding. Small outpouching of fluid along the hepatic margin of the
gallbladder is consistent with focal contained rupture (5:30).  The segment of
colon passing adjacent to the gallbladder is inflamed, consistent with
secondary involvement, but there is no evidence of obstruction.

Two metallic common bile duct stents are in stable position, one of which
originates in the right hepatic ducts and the other of which originates in the
left hepatic ducts. A new internal-external biliary drain enters the right
anterior hepatic ducts and passes through the interstices of the left CBD
stent, terminating in the distal CBD. Left and anterior right pneumobilia
attest to stent patency.  There is persistent obstruction of the caudate lobe
ducts.  There is atrophy of the left hepatic lobe, similar to prior. Two
fiducial markers remain in the right hepatic lobe.  No new hepatic lesion is
identified. A porta hepatis node measures 12 x 9 mm (5:25), similar to prior. 
Retroperitoneal and gastrohepatic ligament nodes are unchanged in size and
appearance.  Hazy opacity adjacent to the SMA (5:30) with small associated
lymph nodes is also unchanged.

The pancreas is unremarkable. Splenomegaly with several punctate granulomas is
unchanged. The adrenal glands and kidneys are unremarkable other than a 1.4 cm
left lower renal pole cyst.

The stomach is normal.  A segment of small bowel in the left upper quadrant is
distended with fecalized contents and a relative transition point in the mid
abdomen (7:14), most consistent with focal ileus. The distal small bowel and
large bowel are not decompressed.

The portal vein remains patent. The intra-abdominal systemic vasculature is
unremarkable.  Small fat-containing periumbilical hernia. No pneumoperitoneum
or free abdominal fluid.  No evidence of peritoneal carcinomatosis.

PELVIS:  Air within the urinary bladder is consistent with recent
instrumentation.  The terminal ureters are normal.  The prostate gland is
unremarkable.  No pelvic side-wall or inguinal lymphadenopathy. No free pelvic
fluid or inguinal hernia.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES: No focal lytic or sclerotic lesion concerning for
malignancy.  Lumbar spine degenerative changes are worst at L4-5 and L5-S1
with intervertebral disk space narrowing and endplate sclerosis.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Acute cholecystitis with small contained rupture along the hepatic margin
of the gallbladder.

2.  Atrophic left hepatic lobe with stable left and right metallic biliary
stents and new internal-external right anterior biliary drain.  No definite
new liver lesion or lymph node with persistent soft tissue around stents at
hepatic ducts confluence.

3.  Left upper quadrant small bowel segmental dilation is likely ileus. 
Clinical follow up recommended.

NOTIFICATION:  The findings were discussed via telephone by Dr. ___ with Dr.
___ on ___ at 1830 ___, 20 minutes after discovery of the
findings.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  Patient with acute cholecystitis with partially perforated
gallbladder.  Need for percutaneous cholecystostomy tube.

PROCEDURE:  Ultrasound-guided percutaneous cholecystostomy tube placement.

TECHNIQUE:  The patient was informed of the procedural technique and its
risks, benefits, and alternatives and the patient gave written consent to
proceed.  A site was marked on the skin in the right subcostal region for an
approach into the gallbladder through the liver.  The site was prepared and
draped in the usual sterile fashion.  1% lidocaine was administered
subcutaneously and down to the edge of the liver capsule.  ___, an 18-gauge
___ needle was advanced under ultrasound guidance through the liver and
into the gallbladder.  Small amount of pus was aspirated from the gallbladder.
___ wire was advanced through the ___ needle and into the
gallbladder and the ___ needle was removed.  The tract was dilated with 6
___ and 8 ___ dilators.  An 8 ___ pigtail catheter was ___
advanced over the wire into the gallbladder under ultrasound visualization,
however, it appeared that the drain when advanced off the metal cannula was
adjacent to the gallbladder between the gallbladder and the liver and
therefore the system was withdrawn.  The ___ needle was ___ reintroduced
under ultrasound guidance in the gallbladder and a small amount of pus was
aspirated a second time.  The ___ wire was ___ advanced through the
___ needle and into the gallbladder.  An 8 ___ catheter with
metal cannula in place was ___ advanced over the winter and into the
gallbladder with position in the gallbladder confirmed under ultrasound
guidance.  The catheter was ___ advanced off the metal cannula and over the
wire and again confirmed to be within the gallbladder.  Pus was aspirated. 
The pigtail catheter was formed within the gallbladder.  The remainder of the
pus within the gallbladder was aspirated.  Position of the tube was confirmed
within the gallbladder under ultrasound with the gallbladder collapsed around
it.  The catheter was fastened to the skin surface with a StatLock.  A
dressing was placed.  Sample was sent to the lab for analysis.  There were no
immediate complications.  

Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of fentanyl for
a total of 125 mcg and Versed for a total of 1 mg throughout the total
intraservice time of 45 minutes by an independent trained radiology nurse
during which the ___ hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored.

FINDINGS:
Images show the gallbladder with large amount of sludge within it and a
thickened wall.  Subsequent images show a needle traversing the liver and into
the gallbladder with subsequently the drain within the gallbladder and ___
the gallbladder collapsed about the drain with gas within the gallbladder
collapsed about the drainage catheter.

IMPRESSION:
Placement of 8 ___ percutaneous cholecystostomy tube into the gallbladder
through a transhepatic approach.  Catheter placed to gravity drainage with
sample sent to the lab.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector axial images were carried out through the abdomen

FINDINGS: 

The major change compared to yesterday's scan is presence of a well-formed
pigtail cholecystostomy tube seen in the right upper quadrant the pigtail
formed in the the gallbladder lumen.  The tube takes a transhepatic course and
there is no local free air or fluid collection. Inflammatory change around the
gallbladder persists but is not increased compared to yesterday's exam.
Similarly, fat stranding around the adjacent colon persists though there is no
evidence of colonic transgression.  There is a small amount of free, simple

tube placement and could be a small amount of bile. This is most mostly
localized around the liver with a small focus seen immediately adjacent to the
hepatic flexure as well. No drainable fluid collection is present and no
subcapsular hematoma or hepatic parenchymal hematoma is seen. Portal vein

The patient has bilateral metallic biliary stents with one extending to the

courses centrally via the interstices of the left-sided stent but loops back

could still be functioning as an external drain but should eventually be
repositioned. At this time, note that the ducts remain decompressed and this
is not new compared to yesterday's study.

The degree of bibasilar atelectasis does not appear significantly different
from yesterday's study.

Unchanged findings includes splenomegaly, small fat containing umbilical
hernia air in the urinary bladder, (presumably status post instrumentation)
osteopenia and lumbar degenerative changes as previously described.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Cholecystostomy tube placed yesterday is positioned within the gallbladder

would be consistent with small, not unexpected bile leak during that procedure
but if symptoms continue, rescanning to assess whether any of this is
developing into a collection could be performed. Even this amount of bile in
the peritoneum can be painful.
2.  Note malposition of distal portion of the right anterior internal/external
biliary drain coiled back on itself in the distal end of the left mental
stent, currently not associated with recurrent biliary obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Johnson. I’m Dr. Patel. I understand you’ve been having fevers again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve had chills and fever off and on for about a week. I hit 102.4 yesterday—that’s when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history with cholangiocarcinoma and recent infections, we’re concerned this could be another episode of cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time? But I finished the antibiotics just a few days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we ordered a CT scan. We need to see if there’s a new blockage or infection source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, the CT shows acute cholecystitis—your gallbladder is inflamed—and there’s a small contained rupture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Rupture? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s contained, so the leak is small and walled off. But it’s infected. We’re starting IV meropenem right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately. Given your cancer and recent treatments, we’ll place a drain through the skin into the gallbladder to relieve the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. We placed a percutaneous cholecystostomy tube. It drained about 100cc of pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pus? So it was definitely infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We sent a sample to the lab to confirm what bacteria are involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You developed a fever and rigors after the procedure, and your lactate went up to 5.5. That’s a sign of severe sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sepsis? Again? I was just in the hospital for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think the procedure stirred up bacteria into your bloodstream. You’re now in the ICU for closer monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the antibiotics handle it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using meropenem and vancomycin for now. Once we get the culture results, we’ll narrow it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your lactate is down to 2.0. That means your body is responding to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The gallbladder fluid grew E. coli. We’re waiting on sensitivity results to confirm the best antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The E. coli is resistant to several antibiotics, including piperacillin-tazobactam. It’s only intermediate to meropenem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Intermediate? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means meropenem might not be strong enough. We’re switching to tigecycline, which the bacteria are sensitive to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve checked. It’s safe. You’ll get it IV every 12 hours for 7 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a PICC line today so you can finish antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: At home? I’m getting better that fast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your vitals are stable, you’re afebrile, and labs are improving. The PICC will let you get IV antibiotics safely at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray after PICC placement showed the tip was too deep—down in the right atrium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause irritation. They repositioned it. The next X-ray shows it’s now in the mid superior vena cava—perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count is down to 4.8. That’s normal. You’re fighting the infection well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the drain? When does that come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You’ll need it for a few months. Interventional radiology will replace it in about three months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bile duct drain? I noticed it’s capped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The imaging shows it’s coiled back on itself but still working. No blockage. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue tigecycline via PICC for 7 days. Keep taking oral vancomycin for C. diff prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain? I’ve been on oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your pain meds as needed. Also keep using stool softeners—your bowels have been slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever, increased abdominal pain, redness or drainage at the PICC or drain sites. Call us if any of those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. All your labs are stable. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Will I see you again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a phone follow-up in two weeks. Also see interventional radiology in three months for the drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my cancer treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished cycle 8. Your oncologist will discuss next steps after you’ve recovered from this infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything you’ve done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. Focus on resting and finishing your antibiotics. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—what about the constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using polyethylene glycol and senna. Drink plenty of fluids. Let your primary doctor know if it doesn’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure and prostate meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue both—atenolol and terazosin—as before. No changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the rosacea cream?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using metronidazole cream as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the DNR status—is that still in place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your DNR status remains. It’s documented in your chart and will be respected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have the discharge papers ready soon. A nurse will go over all the instructions with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow up with everyone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with stage IV cholangiocarcinoma, was admitted with recurrent fevers and found to have acute cholecystitis with a contained gallbladder rupture. He underwent percutaneous cholecystostomy tube placement, which drained purulent material. Post-procedure, he developed fevers, rigors, and a lactate of 5.5, consistent with severe sepsis, and was transferred to the ICU. Blood and gallbladder cultures confirmed E. coli infection, which showed intermediate sensitivity to meropenem. Antibiotics were switched to tigecycline, and a PICC line was placed for outpatient IV therapy. His condition improved with treatment, and he was discharged home to complete a 7-day course of tigecycline, with follow-up arranged for drain management and oncology care.
